newsitem.title: MEXICO: Post-election Mexico model of political politeness.
newsitem.headline: Post-election Mexico model of political politeness.

text.p: Mexico, a country once rife with post-electoral bickering, is bending over backward to be civilized after landmark midterm elections on July 6.

President Ernesto Zedillo, having steered the country through its cleanest elections ever, has barely stopped grinning for a week despite unprecedented electoral losses by his Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

His former foes on the left are seeking to shake off a rowdy image and have been models of good behavior since the elections shot their party to prominence as the second-strongest in Mexico's Chamber of Deputies.

An image of the new harmony graced the front page of every Mexico City newspaper on Tuesday: Leftist leader Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, unwelcome in the presidential mansion for 10 years, was smiling and shaking hands there with a beaming Zedillo.

Cardenas won a landslide victory in the first race in modern times for mayor of Mexico City, and his Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) stunned pundits by seizing the second-biggest bloc of seats in the lower house of Congress.

On Tuesday PRD leader Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador lectured 125 party deputies, including actors, housewives, an aerobics teacher and a bus driver, all swept into power by the unexpected groundswell of support for the left.

His message of strict responsibility, delivered in schoolmasterly tones, marked a new stage for a party that has at times acted undecorously in Congress, heckling the president during his annual state-of-the-nation address and donning piglike face masks to poke fun at his party.

"The conduct of our legislators must be guided by republican morality, with respect for opponents," Lopez said. "For that, we do not need raucous behavior or shouting. ... Firmness and political urbanity are enough."

In the presidential mansion of Los Pinos, Zedillo issued similar orders for his own party to behave itself after the loss of its majority in the lower house, which it had held for 68 years. He urged it to help broker a smooth transition.
"It is our duty to head this political evolution without reticence, without rupture, and without jeopardizing stability and social peace," Zedillo told PRI party chiefs on Tuesday.
The political honeymoon could come to a quick end when the new Congress meets in September and the opposition in the lower house exercises its new powers on such issues as the budget.
To steer its congressional faction through the tough times ahead, the party on Tuesday elected veteran party boss Porfirio Munoz Ledo as its leader in the lower house.
A former PRI official and a fiery orator, Munoz led the PRD during some of its most combative years, at the end of former President Carlos Salinas' term and the beginning of Zedillo's.

The blossoming harmony between the PRD and Zedillo contrasts sharply with the almost warlike attitudes of the past decade. Violent PRD protests followed most local elections, and party leaders branded as radicals by the PRI were shunned in circles of power.
Cardenas, who was a tireless campaigner against PRI electoral fraud for years, spoke warmly of Zedillo late on Monday, thanking him for his support since the elections.

Zedillo, in turn, told Cardenas during their first face-to-face meeting that he would be allowed to pick his own city police chief and attorney general -- appointments still nominally under presidential authority.

In a startling move last week, Zedillo -- a former central banker and fervent free-market economist -- also came close to embracing the PRD publicly. He said he had always believed a strong left wing was in Mexico's interests.
